name: English Learners With Disabilities
title: English Learners With Disabilities
answer: English learners can also have disabilities, and separating a language difference from a disability is one of the hardest judgments in education. AI cannot make that distinction and must never be used to suggest that a student has a disability. Once a student has an IEP, language and special education services must be planned together, with the family included in their own language.

sections.body: This idea addresses students who are learning English and who may also have a disability. A student who struggles to read might be learning English, might have a learning disability, or might have both. Evaluations therefore need to separate language from disability, often by testing in the student's home language. AI tools cannot make this distinction, and they should never be used to suggest one. The problem is that a wrong call can send a student toward the wrong support or deny support they need.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide this practice by grade band, so the approach applies across ages. Once a student has an IEP, the English language development specialist and the special education team should plan jointly. Accessibility tools described in Chapter 12 and the language supports in this chapter can often be combined. The IEP team decides how to combine them, and the family takes part in their own language. A qualified human interpreter should be present at every IEP meeting for a family that needs one.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no formal evidence label for this idea. It cites one finding, from Tang Yan, 2022, that poor interpretation reduces these families' access to special education services and their trust in schools. Beyond that citation, the idea rests on practice and professional judgment rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: AI tools cannot tell language learning apart from disability, so they must never be used to suggest that a student has one. Machine translation is not good enough for decisions as important as special education eligibility or services. A qualified human interpreter should be present at every IEP meeting for a family that needs one. The IEP team decides how language and disability services will work together, and the family takes part in their own language. These decisions stay with people, not with software.
